intro: Christian marriages are governed by the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, divorce by the Divorce Act, 1869, and inheritance by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.

sections.p: A Christian marriage can be solemnised by an ordained minister of religion, a clergyman of the Church of Scotland, a licensed minister, or a Marriage Registrar appointed under the Act.
The man must be at least 21 and the woman at least 18; neither can have a living spouse; and the marriage takes place before two witnesses.
Notice of the intended marriage is given and published; anyone can object on legal grounds. After the ceremony, the marriage is registered and a certificate is issued.

Either spouse can seek divorce for: adultery; conversion to another religion; incurable unsound mind for 2 years; communicable venereal disease for 2 years; not heard of for 7 years; wilful refusal to consummate; not complying with a decree for restitution of conjugal rights for 2 years; desertion for 2 years; or cruelty causing reasonable apprehension of harm.

Spouses who have lived separately for at least 2 years and agree they can't live together can file jointly. The Kerala High Court held in 2021 that a one-year separation is enough, aligning it with other personal laws.
The court can order maintenance during the case and permanent alimony on divorce, considering both parties' means.

If a Christian dies without a will, survived by a spouse and children, the spouse gets one-third and the children share two-thirds equally. Sons and daughters take equal shares (Mary Roy, 1986, extended this to the former Travancore and Cochin areas).
